newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Ashanti open to Anglo deals.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ashanti open to Anglo deals.

text.p: Ashanti Goldfields, the flagship of the Ghanaian economy, said on Thursday it was keeping an open mind on cooperatng with South African mining giant Anglo American.
Ashanti chief executive Sam Jonah said in an interview here he wants Ashanti to remain independent, stressing he did not want Anglo to use its indirect stake to influence the company.
"There is no halfway house. There can be no independence if there is creeping control by one shareholder," he said, adding relations with Anglo were good at the moment.
Jonah's remarks follow reports the Ghanaian government would block any moves by Anglo to effectively control Ashanti. The government has a golden share to prevent a tie-up.
The reports came after Anglo recently acquired a 28 percent stake in Lonrho, the British-based conglomerate that holds 33.6 percent of Ashanti, one of the world's biggest goldmines.
Anglo, keen to expand in Africa, said on Tuesday it would like to develop its relationship with Ashanti, although it was in no hurry to forge any deals.
Jonah, who has worked for Ashanti for 47 years and has headed the company since 1986, said there were no plans for cooperation, although he acknowledged both companies could benefit from it.
Ashanti could learn from Anglo's experience in deep underground mining, while the South African powerhouse could gain from Ashanti's expertise in surface mining and gold processing, he said.
"There could be cooperation to the mutual benefit of the two organisations, but there is nothing on the horizon at the moment," Jonah said.
He added that most of Ashanti's shareholders, among whom are a growing number of U.S. institutions, would like to see the company remain outside the control of any mining firm.
But Jonah also pointed at Ashanti's good reputation in Africa as a reason to stay independent.
"We enjoy tremendous goodwill in a number of African countries...(and) we run the risk of losing that goodwill if our independence appeared to be compromised," he said.
Ashanti, floated in 1994, currently operates in 12 African countries. The company's main asset is the Obuasi mine in Ghana, and has two major development projects in Ghana and Guinea.

Ashanti on Tuesday reported its net profit for the 12-months to September 30 had fallen by 33 percent to $70.9 million. The drop was mainly due to a sharply higher wage bill and rising prices for cyanide, used for leaching gold from ore.
Jonah said Ashanti would use the coming years to consolidate a spate of acquisitions in 1996, which expanded its interest beyond Ghana's borders.
"Ashanti has changed beyond recognition and now we have to optimise our operations in the interest of our shareholders," he said.

Jonah was speaking just after Ghana's president Jerry Rawlings clinched victory in Saturday's presidential and parliamentary elections. Jonah said Rawlings' re-election was good news for Ghana's economy.
"It augurs well for stability and continuity in macro-economic policy," he said. "I think it is good for the investment climate."
